That front book price increase will effectively hit the install base as well. There will be automatic price increases coming in the install base in the back book, driven by the front book.
It's coming in later rather than what other competitors have done. On GHS, look, on GHS, the result was actually impacted. We were more optimistic
We were more optimistic on selling real estate in the last year. Given the commercial market of real estate, I think we have received offers which are not adequate to a fair value, and that obviously had an impact on the real estate generation or sales generation in the GHS segment.
Hannes Wittig
SVP of Investor Relations, Deutsche Telekom AG
Josh you've also seen our guidance for 2024 for ex US and for Germany. The idea that we are shifting costs from Germany and Europe to GHS to make them look better also, I don't think is appropriate, and Christian has explained why GHS results were a bit worse this year. With that, we move on to Emmet at Morgan Stanley, please. George at Citi. Emmet, you are next after that. Thank you.
Georgios Ierodiaconou
Director, Citi
Good afternoon, guys, and thank you for taking my questions. The first one is on fiber and maybe in two parts. Firstly, we've seen in the UK one of the incumbents, in a way, preparing to consolidate the Altnets space. I'm curious with the previous discussion you had, team, around Altnets having issues in some cases with penetration under their financial plans, whether it's something you believe is possible in Germany from a regulatory perspective, something you would pursue if it became available. I just wanted clarification on Hannes' point around the rollout in the MDUs. Obviously, we've seen limited connectivity of fiber customers so far. Is the MDU market different? Is it easier to connect, cheaper to connect, do mass migrations of customers, which you may not be able to do in other parts of Germany?
Just curious if we may see a different trajectory of the homes connected versus past. Then just one clarification on the free cash flow outlook beyond this year. Just these cash returns from the towers, whether it should continue at this EUR 2 billion level in the coming years, or if there's gonna be a change in that. Also, if you could comment a bit for me to understand around the tax situation, if you have already assumed no tax deductibility for 2024 and that could be better or if you would manage that it could get worse beyond 2024 with even fewer tax being deductible. Thank you.
Tim Höttges
CEO, Deutsche Telekom AG
Look, I think, George, to your first question, not an easy task for Deutsche Telekom, because, you know, we have still, you know, a good position on both the copper world and in the fiber world. The Bundesnetzagentur, again, there are two things that we are still market dominant. That is why we are fully regulated in this setup here. Implicitly that says, you know, any kind of consolidation would, let's say, trigger the antitrust offices, cartel offices, you know, to block this kind of activities. Nevertheless, you know, before somebody's going bankrupt of these guys or, if somebody's getting into trouble, it might be good that somebody's operating the infrastructure. Therefore, we are using the passive infrastructure and market that over our infrastructure.
This is clearly yes for everybody who's interested that we are utilizing the infrastructure in these areas. This will help us to reduce the CapEx in these areas as well. The second alternative is definitely that we are trying to approach the authorities if there is a case where somebody wants to divest its infrastructure. I would always try it because, look, I'm not penalizing anybody with this. It's always good for the citizenry in Germany. Everybody who wants to use this infrastructure has the open access to our infrastructure. Therefore, you know, he's not losing something, and it's in the interest of the citizens. Nevertheless, from an antitrust perspective, it looks difficult.
With regard to rollout in MDUs, limited connectivity of fiber customers so far, yes, you're right. This is a little bit, let's say, the German specific that our vectoring, super vectoring network is quite strong. Customers, you know, we have to show them the use cases. They have to understand that this is, you know, creating value for their real estate. We have to show the need of new services coming soon on gaming, on computer, you know, collaboration tools, and as well on HD or UHD TV services. There will be, at one point in time, a super high data demand incoming, so therefore they should be prepared for that. I think our narrative should be to convince customer that they have to upgrade their services here.
The interesting one is, it is easier to connect in some areas? Yes. If you have inferior data throughput in areas, and at, I would say, an inflection point, and we looked academically into this one, of 7x higher speed, which is available, compared to a speed of 16 Mb or around 30 Mb, you know, then that moment it is very easy for customers, you know, to switch over. Let's say it in different words. Where you find inferior infrastructure and you can offer, you know, up to 7x higher speed, customers are switching immediately. You know, you see the elasticity of the service.
That is why we are focusing on areas where, in the rural areas especially, where the data throughput is quite poor, to convince more customers to use the new infrastructure.
Christian Illek
CFO, Deutsche Telekom AG
Let me start with the tax question. What we're currently discussing in Germany is what they call the so-called Wachstumschancengesetz in that they foresee a degressive depreciation opportunity especially for our infrastructure. That degressive depreciation opportunity, if it gets too close, it's currently up in the air, the discussion, will have roughly EUR +50 to 100 million positive impact in 2025 and 2026, but not in 2024. Hannes, you wanna answer the tower question?
Hannes Wittig
SVP of Investor Relations, Deutsche Telekom AG
Yeah, I mean, generally, you know, keep in mind, this was also a question I had online. We expect growing cash tax payments in our ex-US business. It was EUR 1.2 billion cash taxes in 2023. Going forward, we expect this to continue growing. You know, we have talked to you about this already, but do not underestimate that we're not expecting much tax relief beyond what Christian has described, which is a possibility, not a fact at this point, to provide us any shield. In terms of the towers, if I understand the question correctly, you know, we of course clarified that we expect about EUR 0.2 billion of returns from the tower subsidiary this year.
Now, the associate holding that we have here on, of course, half of the tower company. We always expected a shareholder return from the tower company. This is what we told you when we announced the tower deal in July 2022 it was. We also gave a webinar at the beginning of January last year, end of January last year, where we explained how the tower returns would work. We had a tower cash return last year. You know, we treat it as part of the free cash flow ex-US, like we treat the BT dividend, for instance, or other dividends from subsidiaries with one exception. We have not included the dividend we get from T-Mobile.
Strictly speaking, we should because this EUR 1.5 billion we expect this year is actually a repayment for the investments that we have made in T-Mobile that are burdening our interest costs. Keep that in mind when you understand, when you analyze our trajectory in our ex-US free cash flow, because it will reflect the extent to which we own T-Mobile. But for the towers, there's absolutely nothing surprising here. We always said we will get some returns upstream from this business. This is what's happening. There's no recap, just to be clear, right? Maybe this is the confusion today. There's no recap. The tower company has not levered up and given much extra money. This is the regular annual return we were always going to expect and see from the tower company. Okay?
I hope that clarifies it. With that, now we can go to Emmet, who is sharing his impressive collection of impressionist paintings with us. Thanks for that.
Emmet Kelly
Head of European Telecoms Research, Morgan Stanley
Yes. Thank you very much, Hannes. I guess like Usman, I've got one and a half questions or [Foreign language], I think as you say in German. A couple of quarters ago, I asked about data centers and your exposure there. I've kind of got a follow on on that subject, but maybe a little bit more on the cloud side. We're clearly seeing a pretty big change in the geopolitical situation around the world. I know that German B2B and B2C customers, they really value data security, data privacy. With this in mind, I'm just wondering, are you beginning to see any kind of increase in demand from German corporates for a pure sovereign German cloud solution? A product that's provided by a kind of a European company that comes rubber-stamped with data security guarantees.
As a follow on, the half question is related to AI. Obviously a very big day for NVIDIA yesterday. It's kind of like a follow-through from AI into cloud and into data centers as well. Are you beginning to see any kind of demand coming through from German corporates for AI services? Does some of this feed through to systems, or should we expect most of the benefits to go to the hyperscalers? Thank you.
Tim Höttges
CEO, Deutsche Telekom AG
Okay. Starting with the AI question first here. By the way, I will have a keynote speech on AI at the Mobile World Congress on Monday. I will not use it for bashing the regulator. I will do that jointly with Orange, Telefónica, and Vodafone, on a panel. I will talk about AI and, you know, a guide for telcos, you know, to use AI.
I would say, you know, we have today 200 cases with an AI within the company and outside the company, and we have different kind of ways of using it from, you know, taking GenAI and other services to shaping AI by prompting or even, you know, working with other telcos on own LLM services to train the LLM with our own telco-specific data so that it becomes a telco learning system. We are as well productizing AI for our customers. Now there are a lot of initiatives which we have within the company. We see both efficiency gains. We see security elements like anomaly detection areas. We see areas where we can productize.
Now, I expect as well revenues on the B2B side, on this one. Both that we can resell some AI services with us, like Copilot and others, which we anyhow do with Microsoft, but as well that we are developing our own services here. Yes, there is an element now, if this is moving EUR 100 to 150 billion of revenues immediately, Emmet, you know we have to be realistic. It helps that, you know, our B2B area stays on a growth track. You know that we have some aspirations in this area here. I can tell you, we have entirely embraced this AI opportunity here within the company. Follow my presentation. Data center expansion.
I told you that we're investing into data centers, our own with DT Capital Partners. It is as well that you're right in the geopolitical situation, the demand from especially private, you know, services like banking services, financial services, and the public, the governmental services here is high on our offers. That is the area of B2B within the cloud area of T-Systems and where we are focusing on. Look, the issue is we are working here with Google on a partnership in Germany. There's some functionalities where we are still working on coming to market in Q1.
I can go in deeper to this one, but I think maybe we show a detailed view on this one, but this is coming. I see the demand. Now, whether we are really beating the big, you know, hyperscalers, I doubt that because their scale is much bigger. Nevertheless, we expect a significant, you know, growth, which you can then see in the T-Systems numbers already throughout this year in this environment.
Hannes Wittig
SVP of Investor Relations, Deutsche Telekom AG
Excellent. Thank you, very much. I've had two further emails. Thanks, Emmet. From Stefan at Oddo and from Adam at HSBC, who've had problems connecting. Maybe just quickly read them out and give the answer. First, Stefan at Oddo, he's asking if we should expect German earnings trends to be stronger in H2 than in H1. Sorry, H1 than in H2. I got that wrong. Due to various factors, including potentially salary increases, et cetera. Answer would be we like consistency in our German EBITDA trajectory. If we can achieve it, and we are confident we will, then we have a steady earnings development during the year.
Secondly, can you guide us on cash taxes for 2024 and beyond? When will you pay more tax in the US? I think we have talked about the ex-US tax situation already. As far as the T-Mobile is concerned, they would not expect to be a significant taxpayer before 2025. Of course, we also have discussions about extending bonus depreciation in the US, but those haven't concluded. As for Adam, he asked at HSBC whether the BuyIn joint venture could be extended to other partners. Indeed, you know, we have other partners, or the joint venture has other partners, including Proximus, Bell Canada, Odido, and NOS. He asked whether T-Mobile can be included in this partnership.
I think that's something that is being explored. With that, we come to the end of today's Q&A, and I hand back to Tim for any closing remarks.
Tim Höttges
CEO, Deutsche Telekom AG
Look, investors here, look, I like very much, you know, the trajectory where we are. You know, I like very much the 4% and 7%, you know, the growth on service revenues and the EBITDA line, and as well, you know, in line with, let's say, the last years and in line with what we expect for the future. I like very much, you know, that we are very well-financed, you know, with a 10% decrease on our debt side. I like very much that we were able to increase the dividend and the share buyback program within the company.
On top of that, what I like most is the customer growth, because the customer growth is, you know, the guarantee for profitability in next years being at, let's say, 5.6 million customers in the US, 2 million more on the mobile side in Europe, which is very, very strong compared to our competitors. I think I like to flex that. The free cash flow, you know, 41% increase, another strong number this year and another growth coming, you know, with 16% free cash flow growth next year or this year, 2024. I think that's helping. Now, what are we doing here? What is the most important things, you know, until the Capital Markets Day, which is a big event, and by the way, we are already preparing that today.
First, you know, keeping the commercial performance in all the markets where we operating. This is, let's say, well, and by the way, focusing very much as well on the base, a high net promoter score, a high TRIM, high customer satisfaction, low churns, the value sits in our 300 million customer base, and that's an area where we are focusing on. We are very much focusing on new customers in the areas where we have built 5G and fiber. The utilization of the infrastructure is on our highest priority this year.
The allocation of CapEx is something which is very important for us as well this year because a lot of money is, you know, we can allocate, and we have to do it in the right way that we are monetizing that. The higher the utilization of fiber is, the more money we can refund then in other areas. Customer growth is as well coming from B2B. The B2B transformation is going on at a high pace, and I would maybe consider it on the Capital Markets Day before making a bigger deep dive on the B2B and what we're aiming for from a product side here. Emmet mentioned cloud, and he mentioned the data center business.
There are much more on SASE, on security services and other areas, where I see the growth potential already coming in. As well, the tools within the company, the cost optimization, the AI, opportunities which we have in this company. This is something we are intensively working on. We will have, let's say, tariff negotiations with the German workforce coming in Q2. This is a very important point to find a decent, you know, agreement with these partners. Another milestone for us, you know, to deliver on things. You'll find us quite optimistic to deliver on all the capital markets targets which we have laid out last time.
We will do everything to deliver on that one, and we are quite optimistic with regard to the outlook for 2024. Thank you very much, and see you soon.
Hannes Wittig
SVP of Investor Relations, Deutsche Telekom AG
Excellent. So with that, we come to the end of today's conference call. We'd like to thank all those who have participated in this call, and should you have further questions, we kindly ask you to contact our Investor Relations department, and look forward to talking to you again soon. Thank you very much and goodbye.

content.text:
Tim Höttges
CEO, Deutsche Telekom
Yeah. Thank you, Hannes, and welcome to the Q3 2023 results. We continue to deliver consistent growth as promised on both sides of the Atlantic. All businesses are growing. You know that I'm rarely satisfied, but honestly, even I have to find little to criticize in these results, and I'm quite a happy camper today. Let me mention a few highlights today. In the US, we added an industry-leading 850,000 postpaid phone customers, and we raised our outlook for the year. In Germany, we added over 900,000 branded postpaid phone customers in the first nine months. We added 237 broadband customers, and we had the Q1 without any line losses since that last millennium.
Our adjusted core EBITDA grew by 6.8% organically in the first nine months, with 8.9% in Q3. What a number. We pass on T-Mobile's guidance increase and raise our guidance for the third consecutive time this year. I will go through the details later on. Our TMUS stake now exceeds 52%. Our net debt is down around 10% in the last twelve months. In September, T-Mobile US announced a $19 billion shareholders return program, which includes, for the first time, a dividend payment. We are happy to receive the dividend. Starting next year, we also sell into the T-Mobile share buyback. Last week, we also announced our planned shareholder returns for next year.
We plan to raise the dividend by 10% to EUR 0.70 for 2023, and we also announced a DT share buyback of up to EUR 2 billion in 2024. With our planned share buyback, we deliver against our promise to reverse the September 2021 capital increase. Our flywheel remains very successful. Let me now dive into the operations a bit. The foundation is our network. We are network leaders in all our markets now. In the US, our 5G leadership is underpinned by spectrum leadership and confirmed by all the tests. This quarter, we got a clean sweep in every category of network performance for the Q1 in a row from Ookla. There's also no doubt who has the best network in Germany. According to Ookla, our mobile speed is almost twice the competitor average.
We are the network leader in most of our European markets, most recently with wins in Austria, Croatia, Greece, Czech Republic, and Slovakia. We as well lead in customer service. In Germany, our first time resolution rate has doubled in recent years. Now almost two-thirds of faults get solved the first time round. This is ahead of our capital markets guidance. Our complaints are down by 90% in the last four years. In the last three months alone, we won the CHIP and the connect shop test, the FOCUS Magazine service quality test, the connect hotline test, and so on. We had 14 tests from external sources in Germany, and from the 14 tests, we all won them.
You see that we are taking customers at the center of our organization, and this seems to pay off with very high customer satisfaction. By the way, today we as well announced that in all European markets, for the first time in history, we have the highest net promoter score of the competition. Even there, we are fulfilling our promise to make customers first. In Germany, our customer net promoter score neared 20% in October. Our B2B TRIM is at an all-time high, and in the US we had the lowest Q3 postpaid churn ever with 0.87%. The sum is up. It's great to see a strategy which is working. Moving on to page 5 and the development of our organic financials. All segments are contributing to our growth.
Organic group service revenue is up by 3.3%. Ex-US grew by 2.6%. Overall revenues were only flat due to lower equipment revenues. As mentioned, organic core EBITDA increased by 6.8%. In Germany, we posted our 28th consecutive quarter with EBITDA growth, and in Europe, our 23rd consecutive quarter. The foundation of everything we are doing is our network leadership. We now pass 15.6 million European homes with FTTH, up 3.4 million households year-over-year. We passed 6.9 million German homes with FTTH, and we reached our year-end goal of covering 300 million US pops with ultra capacity 5G three months ahead of time. Our strong customer growth continues both in the US and in Europe. Our broadband and TV net adds accelerated strongly this year, driven by Germany.
Let's move on to ESG. At our AGM in April, we had sharpened our climate ambitions. Despite strong growth in data usage, we further reduced our energy consumption on both sides of the Atlantic so far this year by -9%. Let's move to our guidance update. A couple of weeks ago, T-Mobile US raised its guidance for customers, EBITDA, and free cash flow. Today, we are passing this on a group level, and raise our EBITDA and free cash flow guidance by EUR 4.1 billion each. Our ex U.S. guidance, which we upgraded at the H1 stage, remains unchanged this time. Our adjusted EPS guidance for at least EUR 1.60 is also unchanged. We continue to expect 7% core adjusted EBITDA growth this year. Over 40% in free cash flow at group level.
Note that our guidance remains based on a U.S. dollar exchange rate of 1.05 and continues to exclude any contribution from Group Development towers. Please refer to the appendix for a like for like comparison of our guidance with the latest consensus. With that, I hand over to Christian for a deeper dive into the quarter.
Christian Illek
CFO, Deutsche Telekom
Thanks, Tim, and let me start with T-Mobile US. Core EBITDA, according to US GAAP, grew by 12% on a year-on-year basis. If you're interested in how this reconciles into IFRS reporting, I refer you to page 29 in the appendix. The drag from the planned handset leases is coming to an end. It will be around EUR 300 million this year. Let me remind you, in 2020 it was EUR 4.2 billion, and next year, I think it will be almost negligible. The US GAAP, IFRS bridge in this given quarter is EUR 216 million, and we expect it to be EUR 800 to 850 million over the course of the full year. Overall revenues in the US declined because of lower equipment revenues.
Service revenues increased by 3.5%, 3.6%, sorry. That was very much driven by postpaid service revenue growth of 6.4%. You know that we have closed and shut down the wireline business earlier than expected. Without that closure, that service revenue growth would have been 4.6%. What you see in T-Mobile is that our differentiated growth is still continuing to grow. We see a massive expansion opportunity in SMIR, so that means more markets in rural areas. This quarter, for the first time ever, we captured the highest shares of switchers in this market. In business, we have seen the highest net adds in the enterprise space, combined with the lowest churn in history of this business segment.
As you know, we have a very good success in high-speed internet with almost 560,000 net adds in the given quarter, which brings us now to 4.2 million subs. Postpaid phone net adds, not new to you, is 850,000 in Q3, and it was associated with the lowest churn in Q3 ever. Based on the strong customer results, T-Mobile was able to raise its guidance. We now expect 5.7 to 5.9 million postpaid net adds, of which around 3 million will be postpaid phone net adds. I think that brings me to the end of the US section. Let's move over to the very successful German business in Q3.
You see that the organic EBITDA growth was around 3%, 3.1% this quarter. Organic revenue growth improved to 2.1%, driven by service revenue growth, which was 2.4%. We move to the next slide. You also see that the mobile service revenue accelerated to 2.9% growth, and that was coming from both customer growth, so volume growth and upselling. You recall that previous quarters we have been impacted by the Lebara wholesale deal, which we lost, but this is now rolling over. Organic fixed revenues growing by an accelerated 2.1%. What you see in our growth in the fixed service revenue remains very much driven by the retail revenues.
These re-accelerated to 2.4% and was mainly driven by the broadband revenue growth of 5% in the given quarter, relative to the 4% which we have in the previous quarter. The wholesale access revenues grew at 1.6%, remain in positive territory. Despite the fact that we're losing some lines, we're able to offset this by upselling. We currently expect that the fixed service revenues to be weaker in the next quarter for two reasons. One is it's related to content cost accounting. We expect there's gonna be a slight drag relative to the Q4 of the last year. There's a rollover of the single play price increase which we implemented back in October 2022. Let me get to the German fixed KPIs.
As you can see, 96,000 broadband net adds. I think we're benefiting temporarily from the competitor churn, but we are still confident that we have a very strong intake of broadband revenues, broadband net adds, but not exactly at the number you're seeing here. We're also pleased with the acceleration of our TV net adds, which continue to be in the vicinity of 50,000. It was 51,000 in Q3, and this is before the Nebenkostenprivileg is getting to an end. We're also making good progress on upselling. You see that now 45% of our broadband customers have speeds of at least 100 megabits per second. We have around 910,000 FTTH customers, paying customers in our base, which is up 77,000 from the previous quarter.
We also have a pre-marketed contract of around 700 in our books. Our mobile contract customer intake remains strong, as you can see on the next page. 350,000 relative to the 320,000 of the previous quarter. It's coming both from consumer, from the business segment, as well as from congstar. Year to date, we have grown our mobile customer postpaid base by 940,000. What also is encouraging is the strong increase in data usage growth because that supports our more for more strategy. Moving over to Europe. Europe is actually performing better than we anticipated it to be in the beginning of the year. They are coming in with a strong organic revenue growth of 3.7% and an EBITDA growth of 3.3%.
This is despite a very high inflationary cost inflation, which we're seeing in Europe, especially when it comes to salary and energy costs. You can see on the next page the strong commercial performance when it comes to mobile net adds or to broadband net adds. I think it's across all categories, and we're really confident to continue this journey, also in the upcoming quarters. What you also should know is that we are now number one in customer satisfaction measure in TRIM, except for Romania. This is the first time ever that I've seen that number. Moving over to T-Systems. Organic revenues grew by 7% despite a lower order book. The order book is mainly impacted by two factors.
One is obviously the transfer of MMS into the German business, and there's also a lot of phasing, and we will see how this plays out in Q4. Organic EBITDA grew by 1.2%. I think we're fully in line with our guidance, which we have given for the year. I think that is the end of my operational review. Let's get to the group financials. So let me start with the free cash flow. The free cash flow grew by 60% in Q3 on a year-on-year basis, which is largely driven by the significant lower CapEx, which is coming from the US. This is obviously related to the Sprint integration.
It brings us to an overall 25% free cash flow growth year to date, and we'll continue to expect that we are seeing at the end of the year free cash flow growth of larger than 40%. On the adjusted net profit, we actually lost 6% or year to date 14% relative to the previous year. That is very much related to the, what we call non-recurring, non-operational effect, which is related to the provisions for the civil servants for the US Forward, which we had last year, and the fixed price options. They basically gave us a tailwind of almost EUR 0.30 on the share last year, and right now they basically equal out to almost zero. Therefore you see a drag if you compare Q3 2022 to Q3 2023.
Next chart is overall financials. What you can see is financials are impacted by basically three effects. One is obviously the transaction of the tower of our tower business. The second one is the foreign exchange rate. We were budgeting at basically $1 equals EUR 1. Obviously, the dollar is weaker and that puts a burden on the reported numbers. The third one, especially in the US, is a reduction in the handset sales, which basically gives you a negative impact on the revenue figures. Let's move over to net debt. Net debt, actually, what you can see is stable. If you exclude the leases, it's EUR 97 billion. You see how basically the bridge works out with the free cash flow, which is almost reducing net debt by EUR 5 billion.
We have contra effects like the share buyback in the US of 2.5 million, and there's the Forex exchange rate effect, which is putting burden on the net debt. Nevertheless, ex leases we had 2.4 relative to year-end 2022, which was 2.58. Same holds true for including leases. We have now a ratio of 2.94 relative to 3.07 in the end of 2022. We added another chart on the next page, which basically is also taking up some of the discussions which we're seeing right now with you guys and the capital market. It's, which is related to the financing structure of our group.
What you see is basically that we're pretty much having a solid structure. We have a net debt of EUR 170.37 billion, of which EUR 40 billion is leases. The interest-bearing debt is ninety-seven billion, of which 75% is coming from the US. As you know, T-Mobile US and DT have separate debt towers. Let's put them apart in the two sections. What you see is 100% of the refinancing in the US is fixed. It costs us roughly EUR 2.1 billion on a nine-month basis this year. We have an average tenor of 11 years.
In the ex-US business, our maturities are limited to EUR 6.4 billion until end of 2026, and our net debt ex leases is down to EUR 23.7 billion. What you can also see is that we, over the course of the year, have reduced our variable exposure from 41% to basically 8%. There's limited exposure when it comes to future interest rate increases. We're pretty happy with the financing structure. As you can see right now, the average interest rate is around 4%, slightly lower in the ex-US business relative to the US business. I think we're fully funded over the next years. I think we have a very good maturity and a very good interest tenor.
I think this is also reflected by the assessment of the rating agencies. With that, I hand it over to Tim.
Tim Höttges
CEO, Deutsche Telekom
Well done, Christian. Let me wrap up this call by reiterating some high level takeaways. Our commercial performance continues strongly in all markets. Germany has now grown EBITDA for 28 consecutive quarters, the European segment for 23 consecutive quarters. We have raised our full year guidance. We now own more than 52% of T-Mobile US. Our net debt has come down by around 10% in the last 12 months. Based on our strong results, our solid financial framework, and our share of T-Mobile shareholder returns, we were able to propose an attractive remuneration package for our shareholders last week. If you tick the boxes on the Capital Markets Day 2021, you see that we are very well on track with these targets. To summarize it in one sentence I thought about this morning, the one with satisfied customers cannot prevent financial success.
That's the simple, you know, ratio of our quarter this years. But, you know, we stay greedy and hungry and therefore, you know, for us, this is an obligation to even, you know, further accelerate our momentums in all the markets in the business where we are. We are preparing the next capital markets day already quite now. We are currently planning to host our next capital markets day in October 2024. On this one, we are preparing a lot of subjects. Just to give you a little bit of the glance on what we are working on. How can we address global business models in a better way and take advantage of the scale which Deutsche Telekom has gained in the Western world, both in B2B and in B2C?
Talk about including satellites, CPaaS models or even synergies in the operations. What are our new future revenue streams in the core business, but even beyond core? Thinking about AdTech, CPaaS business models, Web3 models, SDX, SASE or other areas. What can we do with fixed line in the opportunity in the U.S. market? How can we define the FTTH market in the next 1,000 days? How can we monetize both fiber and 5G in a better way? We need a change in the mindset from Brussels and from the local regulators as well, that has to change. You know, there is a need for consolidation in Europe. By the way, I don't believe it will help Germany to get a better network by now pimping 1&1, nor with the first auction, nor with now in the second auction, you know.
I do not see why, with him, you know, we would get a better coverage for our people in Germany. Yeah, I don't see it simply there. Anyhow, this is up to the regulators and to the political leaders here, and they took that decision. Now, this leads me over to the 800MHz auction. I think this industry needs every cent, and we talked about that earlier. Every single cent for investments into the infrastructure, into catching up on data throughput. What this industry needs, you know, to fulfill all the AI and all the, you know, the new machine-to-machine services which are rising at high rates. Think about automotive and all the data which goes in and out. Think about logistics.
Think about all the industries which are digitalizing right now. They all go over our network. What we need is spectrum, and more spectrum. We do not need a limitation of spectrum. We do not need another tax on this. Therefore, I think, you know, if Europe wants to catch up, you know, an extension of that auction, maybe with some build-out obligation for 5G standalone or what it might be, I think that makes sense, that is reasonable. Going into an auction, I can tell you, will just take another, you know, pot of money out of this industry, which is needed for the next wave.
Now, with regards to the current discussions here in Germany and 1&1, look, at the end of the day, if the obligations are getting too complex for us and, you know, they are damaging, you know, the business on another angle, I think we should be ready to go into an auction. Deutsche Telekom will defend its position. You know, we will know what we have to do in this one. We will not, you know, let it happen that somebody takes away spectrum which we already today use for serving our customers in a good way. That is, for us, unacceptable. Therefore, you know, then, okay, if they wanna, you know, shoot it out in the market, let's go for it. I'm ready to do this.
I know that maybe some investors don't like that if this is gonna take place, but that's the price which we have to pay to serve customers for a long-term perspective. Sorry for being that direct, but that's my fundamental belief as a leader here.
Christian Illek
CFO, Deutsche Telekom
Tim, I think if we're talking about expansion of the usage, we're not only talking about 800, we're talking 800 and all the other spectrum bands. 800 is not good enough for us at all. Maybe also worth remembering, the Federal Cartel Office doesn't decide here. It's the Bundesnetzagentur, and the Federal Cartel Office has commented on a proposal of the Bundesnetzagentur, right? There are some actual omissions in terms of the recent developments we have seen in the Federal Cartel Office contribution.
Anyway, it's a contribution to a decision that will be taken by the Bundesnetzagentur. With that,
Tim Höttges
CEO, Deutsche Telekom
I think it would be good, guys, if you as investors, as owners of our company, if you could work in the political landscape to say, "Guys, don't take money out of that industry. Don't take spectrum away from these players. You know, extend the use of this auction and then make 2GHz, 6GHz, and millimeter wave available, that even a new player, if he shows up, can have access to spectrum then, the moment he has built a network."
Hannes Wittig
Head of Investor Relations, Deutsche Telekom
Okay. With that we move on to Robert at Deutsche Bank, please.
[Analyst] (Deutsche Bank)
Analyst, Deutsche Bank
Good afternoon, gentlemen. Great going on the energy consumption. Sorry, you can't see me wearing my jumper. Down almost 10% year to date. That's good for costs as well as environment. Please could you remind us what we're looking at for energy cost trends in the ex-US business moving into next year? You've avoided the difficulties of others so far. Can that efficiency momentum be sustained? A quick one on the ex-US balance sheet. Thanks for that improved disclosure. Very helpful. 3.8% cost of debt in Q3. That follows a big switch into fixed debt. Is that fully captured in the 3.8%, so it's a good number going forward? Is that the net interest rate, including inflows from the T-Mobile's shareholder loan? Thanks.
Tim Höttges
CEO, Deutsche Telekom
Go ahead.
Christian Illek
CFO, Deutsche Telekom
Okay. First of all, what we're doing is day in, day out, trying to figure out operational levers in order to bring down the energy consumption per gigabyte being produced. I think this is kind of a collective work which we are sharing across the European segment. The biggest one-off effect you're gonna see in 2024 is the shutdown of the ISAM SDH platform, which is a legacy platform which consumes quite a bit of energy. That's gonna be a big hit, which we don't see in the outer years then, but that's gonna bring us down again. On your cost of debt, 3.8% in that vicinity, maybe 3.9% or something like this is pretty much the refinancing cost which we're having and which we're expecting.
Hannes Wittig
Head of Investor Relations, Deutsche Telekom
Yeah. On the energy cost for next year, we expect broadly stable development for Germany and for the European business. Of course, it's always a bit subject to speculation at this point in time. From today's perspective, we'll expect roughly stable energy costs after an increase of close to EUR 200 million this year. Right. With that, we move on to Andrew at Goldman Sachs, please.
Andrew Lee
Managing Director and Head of TMT Research, Goldman Sachs
Yeah. Good afternoon, everyone. I had two questions. The first question was just on your buyback announcement. Thanks for the color, Tim, on trying to reverse the dilution from 2021. The buyback did, you know, catch the market by surprise a little bit, particularly given comments around your focus on de-gearing. Just wondered if you could talk about your contributing factors into making that buyback decision now in terms of how you think about gearing within the range, anything that changed and that drove you to make the decision when you did on instigating buybacks. Then the second question, apologies for just bringing it up again, there's lots of comments from you, Tim, on the call already on this.
Just in terms of authorities kind of understanding the need to incentivize investment, there's lots of different types of authorities, right? It feels like you have the ear of governments in some markets, regulators have at least adjusted their approach in other markets. The competition authorities, following on from Polo's comments on the German competition authority, in the last day or so they appear more like islands and pretty blinkered, with kind of limited evidence of them changing their approach at all. I wonder if you could just maybe comment specifically on, you know, those comments out of the Federal Cartel Office and which don't really seem to mention investment across the rest of the mobile market, purely on the, you know, new network.
Thank you.
Christian Illek
CFO, Deutsche Telekom
Let me start with the first question, Andrew. Obviously, we're not changing our target. The target remains the same. It's EUR 2.25, EUR 2.75 by the end of 2024. There's quite a bit of uncertainty. For example, if the true-up is kicking in, that influences my leverage by almost 0.1 terms. Not a hundred percent, 0.1 terms, but you see that uncertainty. The second one, I think, which we have to also admit that ex-leases, we are on the old corridor back again. That was the reason why we basically wanted to signal to you guys and show you kind of the proof of the pudding that we're committed to basically bring the capital increase back and start with that share buyback this year.
The targets remain the same.
Tim Höttges
CEO, Deutsche Telekom
Andrew, I met at ETNO conference, two commissioners with my colleagues here from the industry. I had discussion with Thierry Breton. Recently, I met our Vice-Chancellor, Habeck. I was with the Chancellor's office and with the Chancellor recently. I was with our minister for infrastructure the other day. I can tell you, everybody, every single politicians admitted that they have to change the setup for our industry. It is not that they are like I was at the beginning, you know, I'm 25 years now in this industry. At the beginning, they said, "You're these bad guys, we have to do something about you. You, your margins are too high and, you're screwing customers," blah, blah. It's the opposite. Everybody is there and trying to find a way to even up the situation.
Now, the problem is, there are a lot of voices. There are newcomers in the market, there are challengers, because if they change something, there are always winners and losers. If you allow consolidation, smaller companies might have a problem with that. Therefore, this is, I think, the orchestra which you hear right now everywhere. Everybody of these political leaders want to find. I think it's a governance issue to get this orchestra coordinated in the right way, finding the way on the legislation, finding a way to get this passed. It's not like a company.
It's not like when we have a policy and we wanna bring that through, we decide it, and then it takes place. It has to get orchestrated. With the elections, with all the changes, it takes a little bit longer, but I think, you know, we have passed an inflection point here. They want to change it, they want to improve it, but they have not found really the key and the way going forward, and therefore, I think it will come over time. The question is how can we accelerate that process? That is what I'm trying to do.
Hannes Wittig
Head of Investor Relations, Deutsche Telekom
Great. Thanks, Tim. We've got five more questions or five more people who want to ask questions. Let's be tight. We start with James at New Street, please.
James Ratzer
Partner and Head of European Communications Services Research, New Street Research
Yes. Good afternoon, Tim and Christian. Thank you, Hannes. Yes, I have two questions, please. The first one was just to revisit your capital structure and in particular, how you're thinking about the dividend within that. I mean, also you've put up some great numbers. You're gonna have a 10% dividend growth, which is fantastic. At the same time, your payout ratio, I think, will be in the lower half of your 40% to 60% ratio. Is that because of the fact that you're gonna be like at the very high end of the 2.25 to 2.75 times leverage target? Could you see a scenario as you de-lever the business that you can start to move the dividend into the upper half of that payout range? Then the second question I had, please, was just regarding your broadband pricing.
I mean, in Germany, I understand you can't comment on future moves to come. If I look at what's happened in the past, you're seeing about 5% broadband growth, 2% customer growth roughly implies about 3% ARPU growth. Is that coming now from back book customers that you are getting them to trade up? You know, given the moves you've made on the front book, is it now you're seeing new customers you're winning, coming on at prices above the overall ARPU? Would just love to understand some of the mixes you're seeing in the current ARPU trends in the business. Thank you.
Tim Höttges
CEO, Deutsche Telekom
We traded dividend growth also against the share buyback discussion which we had in this announcement. From this perspective, if there is opportunity, obviously the dividend can benefit from a payout ratio aside from the EPS growth which we're gonna see. On the broadband pricing, what we're seeing right now is, as you said, there's a volume element, and this quarter was a very strong volume element because of the back book pricing of our competitors. There were customers fleeing away from the other guys and joining us. What you can see is like, I think you can see with the 45% penetration of broadband customers beyond 100 megabit, this continuous more for more trend is almost a linear curve, and we expected it to be a linear curve in the future as well.
We're giving customers what they need. They can actually have more. That's also one of the reasons why we don't see this massive shift into fiber right now, because Germans tend to buy what they need and not more than what they need. We expect that the more for more strategy will continue to grow, and there will be an element of share gain, especially in the retail space, which will support the broadband growth.
Hannes Wittig
Head of Investor Relations, Deutsche Telekom
Great. With that, we move on to Mathieu at Barclays, please.
Mathieu Robilliard
Senior Analyst and Managing Director, Barclays
Yes, good afternoon, and thank you for taking the question. I had two, please. In terms of share buyback. So, Tim, you qualified the share buyback that you announced by saying that you're delivering on the promise to offset the dilution linked to the US deal. Does that mean that you only considered share buybacks in the future in these same circumstances, or that you think more broadly that it's a good way to return cash to shareholders? The second question was with regards to DISH. I think DISH is due to make a payment for spectrum that you handed to them. I think there's some delays. I guess the question was, when do you think you'll have visibility on a potential payment?
Whether or not that payment, which I think is EUR 3.5 billion, is included in your guidance to delever the company or that could be a potential upside. Thanks.
Tim Höttges
CEO, Deutsche Telekom
Look, Mathieu, I think, you know, there's a philosophical discussion behind your question. You know, can you manage with the passive side of a balance sheet, you know, the value of a company? What is the contribution of a share buyback? I like dividends, by the way, because dividends are clear, you know, yield and an interest which you pay out for your shareholders. I like dividends because they're clear commitment, they are lasting. In our industries, I think they are committing long-term investors longer into a company than, you know, share buybacks coming and going. There are good arguments for share buybacks as well. Look, I don't wanna go into this philosophical discussion.
I think this is something for a bilateral discussion. What I wanna say here right now is we have made now a big step forward with regard to this dilutive effect. Now the question should be, what are you doing beyond that? There's no decision taken. It always depends on the commercial situation. It always depends on our debt situation within the company. If you ask me, do you have the intention to take the second part of the dilution out of the market with an instrument like a share buyback? I would say, yes, I have the intent. I would support that. Now, that is not something we have decided yet, but that is at least, you know, the way forward.
There's some, you know, water which will go down the Rhine throughout this period until we have executed on this one. I hope that then we have a debate with you investors. You know, what you like more, share buybacks or dividends, where we should go and what you like. For me, the main headline is a proper, sustainable, long-term growing capital allocations with my shareholders. This is, let's say, the way forward and how we then design that's for discussion.
Christian Illek
CFO, Deutsche Telekom
On the 3.6 MHz question, look, as you know, the time has been extended to 1 April. T-Mobile US will receive $100 million instead of $72 million from DISH. DISH has time up until 1 April to decide whether they want to acquire the spectrum, yes or no. You have seen the DISH numbers. I think they have decreased the option value for the spectrum by 10% or something like this, if I'm not mistaken. I can answer you the second part of your question, but we're not public with this. Whether it's part of the planning envelope, yes or no, therefore, please respect that we don't make this public here.
Hannes Wittig
Head of Investor Relations, Deutsche Telekom
Well, as you know, we have a prudent plan, and I guess it's not in the consensus anyway. With that, we move on to Steve at Redburn, please. Steve?
Stephen Malcolm
Analyst, Redburn Atlantic
Thanks, Hannes. Tim, in the past, you've rightly criticized this for being a little bit too hard to please at times. Just to prove that leopard can change his spots. First thing I never do, which is well done, a very good set of numbers. Q3 looks very, very good. I've not gone through all the details yet, but looks very good all over the place. A couple of questions. One is just on the ex-US leverage. Can you help us understand, you know, how much time you spend looking at that and what you think the right sort of leverage corridor is, and will you review it, you know, when you hit the target the rating agencies set out for you?
Obviously, you know, your ex-US cash and the dividends you get from the US and tendering shares in the buyback should see debt continue to fall. Should, you know, you expect EBITDA to rise. It looks like that EBITDA is falling sort of mid-high ones there. Is that the right place for that business? That's question one. Just coming back to the question asked by David on US fiber. I guess sort of capital light sounds pretty seductive, but at the end of the day, you're gonna rely on altnets to do that. You have direct experience of altnets in Europe. I mean, DT's, DTCP's got an interest in a couple of Community Fibre and ODF. From the outside looking in, they're not doing terribly well.
You need to get to 40%, 50% penetration to make these things work. Do you think that's it? What particularly is different about the US that you think can make that work? Is it just the T-Mobile brand, the fact that you think you can, you know, use that to get very high penetration rates? Or is there anything else that you think, you know, can sort of give that real heft? Because it feels from the outside looking in, that it's a very kind of, you know, marginal solution to what could be a bigger long-term issue around broadband connectivity. Thanks.
Christian Illek
CFO, Deutsche Telekom
Okay. Let me answer the ex-US leverage question with a lot of ifs. If the share buyback in the US continues in the way how it is right now. If there will be no significant M&A beyond what Tim is indicating. If we're not significantly increasing the dividend. If we're not continue with the share buyback, and you heard the intent to basically at least bring the dilution to zero, then obviously the ex-US business will significantly delever. These are all decisions which we haven't taken now. The only decisions which we have right now basically extends into 2024, and there you don't see that significant deleveraging yet. If you assume all these assumptions I just mentioned, yeah, there will be a significant deleverage on the ex-US side.
Tim Höttges
CEO, Deutsche Telekom
Even the second question, just fiber. Look, I'm not so concerned with regard to the US market in comparison with the European market, on the altnets side. Because the market situation, by the way, as it is in other areas as well, is totally different. First, we have regional monopolies. So you do not have, let's say, multiple infrastructures. The monopolist always have very high prices. In the US, you know, the ARPU of, you know, Comcast and the like, you know, it's sometimes triple digit. So if you wanna compete in this market, you know, you have a lot of headroom, you know, to challenge them. Then, you know, these big monopolies are coming with super high costs from their system.
If you look to smaller players, to greenfield operations, you know, they have significantly lower cost. On top of that, you know, if there would be an over-penetration, yes, I would be worried, but this market is very fresh and young. We're just at the beginning of a fiber penetration in the US. Therefore, there's a lot of room. On top of that, apart from the high ARPUs, which you can get to amortize this infrastructure, I think we should as well see that there's as well a hunger for higher data throughput. You see that with our super success on fixed mobile substitution services, which we have in the US, with this very low inequalities.
If you come with superior infrastructure, there are a lot of areas where you can really differentiate against the cable cos. On top of that, we have the US brand, which is well recognized. Most of the markets, Mike said it, we have a market leadership position and a great distribution. We have to manage more the processes. We have to get this up and running. We have to establish the skills in our ecosystem. That is, I think, the main task. I'm less worried about
that the alt-nets might not get their strength in this ecosystem. The market is totally different from its economics.
Hannes Wittig
Head of Investor Relations, Deutsche Telekom
Okay, before we move on to Ottavio with his questions. Just quickly, I was told that the one question from James was a bit. The answer was mute, so therefore I'd just like to go back to it. Christian was asked if we move into the leverage comfort zone, we might consider to have a dividend payout in the upper half of our payout, stated payout ratio. Christian said that's definitely a possibility. For those who missed it because he was muted at the time, that's what you would have missed. Anyway, with that, we move on to Ottavio, please.
Ottavio Adorisio
Research Analyst, Societe Generale
Hi, good afternoon. Thanks for taking questions. A couple from me. The first is for Christian, and it's basically related to slide 24. You've already gone back a couple of times. When I look at the interest rate payable on that you pay on your debt and the TMUS pay on their own, of course, yours looks lower. But if one take into account that the US has much longer maturity, they have a lower credit ratings, and they have a high underlying sovereigns, much higher in the US than in Germany. I was just wondering it's the US been so good or is the fact that they've been so good on the timing when they did the refinancing. Therefore, do they have any flexibility?
Because you already commented about the 3.9 you expect on the refinancing that you could optimize that 3.9 a bit down, or you reckon that's basically that will be the floor on the refinancing you expect. The second one is for Tim. It's specifically on the FTTH rollout. Now, if you remember on the Capital Markets Day, we were looking for 2 million FTTH lines as sort of targets on the rollout. Now you're targeting 2.5, so effectively you're doing better and you improving in terms of the coverage. We never heard from Deutsche in terms of where you want to end up. Now we probably have to wait in the Capital Markets Day next October next year. But if you can give us a bit of an idea.
You've quantified in the past that you will be bringing FTTH where it's economically sensible to upgrade. If you can tell us how much of Germany is economically sensible to upgrade as of today. Thanks.
Christian Illek
CFO, Deutsche Telekom
Let me start with the first question. First of all, on the US, let me just comment on the US I think in hindsight, the US was super lucky with their timing on refinancing as we closed the deal, as you know, because the interest rates were really low. The second one, I think, they are benefiting from retiring old high yield bonds by paying them back, which is coming in with a significant higher interest rate than what they have to refinance right now. For example, in the last quarter, they retired bonds, which costed them close to 8%, while at the same time they refinance at 6%, 5.8% or something like this. This is the benefit which the US is having.
I'm not 100% sure whether I can answer this question on the ex-US side precisely. I have to go back if the answer is not correct. I think we're staying at that level. Coming back to the previous question from Steve, if we're deleveraging, obviously then the interest costs will come down because our refinancing will come down. Whether the rate is coming down, I would be surprised, but let me go look it up and if there's a significant change, we will inform you about this. Okay?
Tim Höttges
CEO, Deutsche Telekom
Ottavio, I love your question. By the way, some headache around that one. The first thing is, you know, we have said that we're gonna make 10 million households by the end of 2024. What I will confirm here right now with all my conviction is, you know, we were gonna deliver on this one. That is the issue. Now you can say, by the way, we have 2.5 million this year. You've heard me saying I love to see 3 million. Yeah, so I'm on the gas pedal here. I love that. So therefore, you know, we were faced by shortage in construction capacities in Germany.
By the way, which I don't understand, that we don't find sufficient construction people here because there must be capacities due to the interest rates in the housing area, but nevertheless, we have a shortage here. The second, we have inflationary costs. We wanted to manage down. Remember the productivity which I promised once, you know, down the cost to something around EUR 1,000 per household. Then facing the inflation, we were not able to really, let's say, get that task managed properly. Therefore, you know, we are facing a tough environment these days to deliver at cost on target here in these circumstances.
Look, as we always had planned it more conservative, the EUR 10 million is not at risk at all. Second part of your question is, we do not know where you're aiming for. Look, the political target is 50% by 2025 and 100% by 2030. I think this is possible. We will have in this ecosystem, including our partners by the way, I always include our EQT partner and always the Deutsche Glasfaser into this one. GlasfaserPlus into this one. We will aim for the same ownership economics as we have had it in the copper area. This is what we are striving for. This is something like 75% of infrastructure, which we should own, and which we should control.
This is, let's say, our ambition on the long-term horizon. By doing this, we can guarantee a growing business for our owners. Because we do not wanna build our business model on wholesale alone. We have seen that in France, you know, with shrinking revenues and EBITDA due to the fact that you only have a wholesale revenue on this one. Therefore, we have said, "Look, we should have the same owners economics as we have had it in the copper environment in the fiber." This is an orientation. It is nothing which is now nailed in a plan because our plan is a four-year plan and not a longer term perspective. If you wanna have an orientation, that's the one I can give you.
Hannes Wittig
Head of Investor Relations, Deutsche Telekom
Excellent. That brings us to the last question for today or questions from Adam at HSBC, please. Adam?
Adam Fox-Rumley
Telecoms Analyst, HSBC Bank Plc
Thank you. Thanks very much. Actually, it was a bit of a follow-up to that last question on fiber in Germany. I'd be interested now. You've got, you know, more than 900,000 homes connected. How you're seeing the cost to connect or the processes to actually connect homes evolving, whether you're seeing any change there. I guess a related question, whether or not you're seeing any change in the pace of rollout kind of on the streets from your network-based competitors at the moment. Thanks.
Tim Höttges
CEO, Deutsche Telekom
By the way, the most important thing, you know, with regard to the 900,000 paying customers in Germany on the fiber infrastructure is that their net promoter score or their TRIM values is higher than all the other products which we are selling. We have happy customers, and that is the most important thing. By the way, just this minute I got, you know, a mail here on this number. This is for me a very important note. On the cost side, Christian, I think it's a mixed bag of build-out period for quite a while now.
Hannes Wittig
Head of Investor Relations, Deutsche Telekom
Yeah.
Tim Höttges
CEO, Deutsche Telekom
I think our ambition was, you know, to get the cost unit down by 25% to below 1,000 per home passed. That was our initial planning, which we laid out in the earnings. We are definitely seeing a cost inflation on the in-fiber construction areas in the order of magnitude of 20%. Therefore, you know, I would say we are still something between 1,000 and 1,500 EUR per homes passed, which we're currently facing here. We have taken decisive actions to manage this. For instance, we have now 1,000 people hired in the organization for construction area purposes, much cheaper than if we would buy them outside.
To be honest, I'm expecting overall in the mixed bag, you know, an average cost per home below EUR 1,000, still our ambition for the upcoming period. I think this is something which we have to lay out in more detail in our Capital Markets Day perspective, and giving you all the facts to this one that you can build your models on it.
Christian Illek
CFO, Deutsche Telekom
Ottavio, I got a reconfirmation from my treasurer, from Stefan Deman, that interest rates are expected to be at that level, 3.8%, if we go for new financing based on fixed, so not a lot of changes.
Hannes Wittig
Head of Investor Relations, Deutsche Telekom
Just maybe on following up on Adam's questions. The EUR 1,000 that Tim referred to is the cost of passing homes, which bakes in a certain level of connections. When it comes to the connection in Germany, the connection per home has a huge range, so it's very hard to give averages on this one, and we haven't disclosed them. In terms of the rollout pace, we estimate that this year we will build out round about two-thirds of the homes in Germany that are being built this year.
Okay. With that, we come to the end of our conference. We'd like to thank you for participating in this call. Thank you, Tim and Christian. If you have further questions, we kindly ask you to contact our investor relations department. We look forward to hear from you soon. With that, goodbye.
Tim Höttges
CEO, Deutsche Telekom
Bye everybody. Thank you.
Christian Illek
CFO, Deutsche Telekom
Thank you.
Operator
Thanks for using WebEx. Visit our website at www.webex.co.uk.

content.text:
Tim Höttges
CEO, Deutsche Telekom
Yeah. Thank you, Hannes, and welcome to the Q1 2023 Results Call here. We had a good start to the year. Customer growth and financials were in line or even better than we expected. We're stepping up our 2023 guidance, and our leverage has taken a big step down. We are now at 2.9x including leases, and at 2.3x excluding leases. We achieved the majority in T-Mobile US, which we have noted already. We continue to deliver consistent growth, by the way, in all our businesses as promised.
Let me go through some highlights before Christian will then deeper dive into the quarter. Our growth continued in the Q1. All segments contributed here. Organic group service revenue grew by 2.6%, ex-US it grew by 2.2%. The organic core EBITDA, ex-handset lease revenues, increased by 4.4%, ex-US by 4.6%. The ex-US EBITDA growth was impacted by cost phasing in GHS, and we expect it to re-accelerate in the coming quarters.
Germany has now delivered 26 consecutive quarters of organic EBITDA growth, the European segment 21 quarters. I've asked for the US, but Hannes couldn't deliver it because, I think, it's something in the vicinity of 40 quarters. You see, all areas on growth and T-Systems are growing. Total organic revenue were down year-on-year, and that is something we're gonna explain later. The main driver of it is explained by 20% lower US equipment revenues, which we don't have after the Sprint merger has been accomplished.
The decline mainly reflects two temporary effects. The first, our planned unwind of handset leases, which constitutes a headwind of more than 1%. The second is the anniversary of particularly strong handset sales last year, when we seeded the Sprint base with handsets that functioned on our network. Both of that are not recurring in the future and therefore, we see the decline in our group revenues. Moving to the networks. The foundation of our growth remains our network leadership and all the investments we have taken here.
We now pass almost 14 million European homes with FTTH, up by 3.1 million households, year-on-year. We passed 5.7 million German homes with FTTH now.
